home.heroEyebrow: Understand · Know your options · Get help
home.heroLead: Most government decisions can be reviewed. We cover decisions by the Australian Government (Commonwealth) and the State of Victoria. What Now? turns your letter into plain English, your options into a numbered list, and your next step into a letter — free, no account, nothing stored.

home.howStep2Body: The review paths open to you, with the official sources we used.

home.trust2Body: Every answer shows where it’s from.

home.helpBody: Free help is one tap away — government, tribunals, and community legal centres.

home.learnTitle: Two ways to challenge a decision —
home.learnLead: Merits review and judicial review are the two public-law paths for challenging a government decision. Most people have never heard of them. We explain both in plain English: what each one is, who hears it, and the grounds of judicial review that people raise. It is free, and built to be easy to follow.

home.limitBody: Most reviews have a time limit set by the law for your decision. We show it with the official source — never as a countdown, never in red. There is still time to get help.

home.slotBody: Answer the three questions and the ready-to-send letter goes here — yours to keep, or to hand to a free service.
home.humansBody: Talk to a person whenever you like — they can take it from here.
home.coverageLead: We cover two governments in detail. If your letter came from either one, you are in the right place. Each has its own tribunal for merits review and its own court for judicial review.
home.covCthBody: Centrelink and Services Australia, child support, the tax office, and other federal agencies. Merits review is at the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART). Judicial review is in the Federal Court.
home.covVicBody: Fines and infringements, renting and notices to vacate, public and social housing, councils and state departments. Merits review is at VCAT. Judicial review is in the Supreme Court of Victoria.
home.covFoot: In another state? The two paths work the same way, so the guides still help — and we always point you to a free service near you.

rights.routeTitle: Please talk to a free legal service
rights.routeBody: Because of what you told us, this is best handled by a person, not a self-help path. These free services can help:
rights.avenueMRWhat: A tribunal can look at the decision again and may change it.
rights.avenueJRWhat: A court can check whether the decision was made in a lawful way.
rights.noReview: A formal review may not be available
rights.fallbackNote: We matched this to a general guide. The details of your decision matter, so it is worth checking with a free service.
rights.learnLead: What each path means, in plain English. Open whatever is useful — you don't have to read it all.
rights.learnMore: Read more about how review works
rights.groundsLead: For court (judicial) review, people point to a specific problem with how the decision was made. Tick anything that sounds like your situation — it will be added to your summary as points to mention. This is general information, not a judgment about your case.
rights.reasonsLead: You can ask the decision-maker, in writing, why they decided the way they did. Here is a draft you can edit and send yourself.
rights.handoffTitle: Take this to a free service
rights.handoffLead: We can make a short summary of your situation to bring to a community legal centre or lawyer. It is made on your device and is not stored.
rights.privacy: Nothing you enter here is stored.
rights.flagFamilyHint: Tick this only if the decision is one of those. If you have a health condition or children, but the decision is about Centrelink, housing, renting or a fine, leave it blank.
rights.urgentTitle: Please call a free service today
rights.urgentBody: You can still read your options below. Bring them to the call — it makes the conversation faster.
rights.analysisLeadBoth: Two paths are open for this decision. Most people look at merits review first, because a tribunal can change the outcome. A court is different: it checks whether the decision was made lawfully, and it can send the decision back to be made again.
rights.analysisLeadMerits: Merits review is open for this decision. A tribunal can look at your case again and make a different decision.
rights.analysisLeadJudicial: Merits review does not appear to be available for this decision. Judicial review asks a court to check that the decision was made lawfully.
rights.analysisLeadNone: A formal review may not be available for this decision. A free service can check that with you, and there may still be other options.
rights.focusMerits: The tribunal is not only asking whether the original officer got it wrong. It looks at the facts again, as they stand now, and decides what the correct or preferable decision is. So what carries weight here is evidence about your situation — documents, dates, letters, and anything that has changed since the decision.
rights.focusJudicial: A court is not deciding whether the outcome was harsh or unfair. It looks at how the decision was made. So what carries weight here is the process — what you were told, what you had a chance to respond to, and what was or was not taken into account. Judicial review starts from a named ground of review.
rights.stepsLead: These are the usual steps people take. You can stop at any point, or hand the whole thing to a free service.
rights.step1: Ask for the reasons in writing
rights.step1Body: Reasons tell you what was taken into account. That is what both paths turn on. A draft is ready below.
rights.step2Body: Letters, dates, records, and anything that has changed since the decision.
rights.step3: Lodge with {body}, within the time limit
rights.step3Body: The time limit for your decision is named above, with its official source.
rights.step4Body: They can check the path, confirm the date, and take it from here if you want them to.
rights.faqLead: Plain-English answers written for this kind of decision.
rights.applyLead: If you decide to go ahead, here is a draft you can edit and send yourself. Pick the path you mean — the two letters say different things.
rights.applyMeritsHint: This letter asks a tribunal to look at the decision again on the facts and make the correct or preferable decision.
rights.applyJudicialHint: This letter is about how the decision was made, not the outcome. Judicial review is a court process and it is technical, so this is a starting point to take to a free legal service.

privacy.title: Your privacy
privacy.intro: This service is built so that we don't keep your letter or your answers.
privacy.point1: Your letter is read on the spot to explain it, then discarded. We don't store it on our servers and we don't log what it says.
privacy.point2: There's no account and no login. Anything kept for your convenience stays on your own device, and you can clear it any time.
privacy.point3: We don't put your personal details into analytics.
privacy.point4: When you connect with a free legal service, you deal with them directly under their own privacy rules.

about.title: About this service
about.intro: This is a free service that helps people understand and respond to government decisions.
about.infoNotAdvice: This service gives general information, not legal advice, and cannot tell you what will happen in your case. For advice about your own situation, talk to a free legal service.
about.groundedBody: Every answer is grounded in a checked set of rules and points to where it comes from. When something isn't covered, the service says so and points you to a person who can help — it never guesses.
about.currencyBody: Rules and time limits change. Each entry carries the date it was last checked, and entries are reviewed on a regular cycle.

consent.message: We use privacy-friendly analytics to understand how the service is used. No personal details are collected.

tour.replayDone: Guides reset — open a step to see them
tour.whoOptionsText: This one answer sets your whole path. A federal decision and a state decision are heard by different bodies, so we ask first and then only show you what fits.
tour.privacyText: Your answers stay on your device. There is no login, and we never keep your letter or what you tell us.
tour.areaText: It does not have to be exact. If nothing fits, choose the general option — you will still get the review path and free help.
tour.dateTitle: The date helps, but it is optional
tour.dateText: If you have the letter in front of you, the date on it lets us show timing information that fits your situation.
tour.tripwireText: These are situations where a person, not a self-help tool, should help you. Tick one and we stop and take you straight to a free service.
tour.consentText: We give general information, not legal advice, and we cannot tell you what will happen in your case. Tick to say you understand, then continue.
tour.avenueText: A tribunal can look at the decision again and may change it. A court checks whether it was made lawfully — not whether it was a good decision.
tour.reasonsText: This is a ready-made letter asking the decision-maker to explain their reasons. Copy it, edit anything you like, and send it yourself.
tour.groundsText: Tick anything that resembles what happened to you. It becomes a list of points to raise with a lawyer — it is not a judgement about your case.
tour.handoffText: This makes a short summary of your situation to bring to a free legal service, so you do not have to explain it all from scratch. It is built on your device.
tour.askInputText: Plain language works best — write it as you would say it. There is no need for legal terms.
tour.askSubmitText: We only answer from a checked set of rules, and we show you where each answer came from. If your question is not covered, we say so and point you to someone who can help.
tour.decodeUploadTitle: A photo of the letter is enough
tour.decodeUploadText: Take a picture or upload a PDF. We read it on the spot to explain it, then discard it — the letter is never stored.
tour.decodePasteText: If it is easier, type or paste what the letter says. You do not need the whole thing — the main paragraphs are plenty.
tour.decodePrivacyText: We never keep your letter. Close the tab and nothing about it remains.
